stem: This question is about religion, healing and modern medicine.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how Indigenous Religion and Christianity understand illness and healing.

points.description: Indigenous Religion: illness is understood to have natural, spiritual and social causes, which are considered together
Spiritual causes include displeasure of the ancestral spirits (midzimu/amadlozi) when a ritual is neglected, and an angry spirit such as ngozi
Social causes include family quarrels and harm believed to be done by witchcraft, though accusations have caused suffering
The n'anga or inyanga diagnoses the cause, using divination, prescribes herbs and may advise a ritual such as a bira ceremony to restore harmony
Healing aims to restore harmony between the person, the family and the spirit world, and responsible healers refer serious illness to the clinic
Christianity: the Gospels report that Jesus healed many people (for example Mark 2:1-12; Mark 10:46-52), seen as signs of God's compassion and examples to follow
James 5:14-15 tells elders to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil; Catholic and Orthodox churches keep the Anointing of the Sick as a sacrament
Churches heal through prayer and healing services (Pentecostal), prophets, holy water and blessed objects (AICs), and through mission hospitals and clinics

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In Indigenous Religion illness is understood to have natural, spiritual and social causes, which are considered together. Spiritual causes include the displeasure of the ancestral spirits (midzimu in Shona, amadlozi in Ndebele) when a ritual has been neglected, and an angry spirit such as ngozi. Social causes include quarrels in the family and harm believed to be done by witchcraft, although accusations of witchcraft have caused great suffering.

The n'anga or inyanga is consulted to find the cause. The healer uses divination, prescribes herbs and may advise a ritual such as a bira ceremony. The aim is to restore harmony between the person, the family and the spirit world, and responsible healers refer serious illness to the clinic.

In Christianity the Gospels report that Jesus healed many people, for example the paralysed man in Mark 2:1-12 and blind Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46-52, which Christians see as signs of God's compassion and examples to follow. James 5:14-15 tells the elders to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches keep this as the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick. Churches heal through prayer and healing services in Pentecostal churches, through prophets who use holy water and blessed objects in African Independent Churches, and through mission hospitals and clinics.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed point, one for the social causes. Credit any accurate description and mark the best points up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: To what extent can religious healing and modern medicine work together?

points.description: They can cooperate: churches run mission hospitals and clinics, and responsible healers refer patients with serious illness to the clinic
Judaism (pikuach nefesh), Islam (the body is a trust; treatment is encouraged) and most churches support medicine
Religion offers comfort, meaning and community support, so patients receive care of the whole person alongside treatment
They can conflict when a belief replaces treatment, for example when a group discourages vaccination or clinic visits; a child has a right to health care (Constitution, sections 76 and 81)
A supported conclusion

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Religious healing and modern medicine can work together to a large extent. Churches run mission hospitals and clinics, and responsible traditional healers refer patients with serious illness to the clinic. Judaism teaches pikuach nefesh, that saving life comes first, Islam teaches that the body is a trust and encourages treatment, and most churches support medicine.

Religion also offers comfort, meaning and the support of a community, so the whole person is cared for alongside treatment.

However, they can conflict when a belief replaces treatment. When a group discourages vaccination or clinic visits, children may be left unprotected, and children have a right to health care under the Constitution. I therefore conclude that the two work together well in most cases, and the risk arises only when belief replaces treatment. Families are safest when they combine prayer with the advice of a trained health worker.

parts.explanation: Level marking: developed examples of cooperation and of conflict, and a supported judgement, reach the top levels.

explanation: A Paper 2 style question: (a) describe understandings of healing, (b) assess how far religion and medicine can cooperate.
hints: In (a) describe both religions with named practitioners and texts. In (b) give cooperation and conflict, then judge.

stem: This question is about religion and HIV and AIDS.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how religious organisations in Zimbabwe respond to HIV and AIDS.

points.description: Prevention messages: teaching abstinence before marriage and faithfulness within marriage, and encouraging voluntary testing
Religions differ on condoms: the Catholic Church teaches abstinence and fidelity, while many other churches and Muslim and Jewish teachers accept them for protection
Testing and treatment: church and mission clinics offer testing and ART, and congregations announce clinic days
Home-based care: volunteers visit the sick, help with food and washing, and support families
Care for orphans and vulnerable children: school fees, food and counselling
Support groups for people living with HIV, often held in church or mosque halls
Speaking out against stigma, teaching compassion (Matthew 25:35-40; James 1:27; Qur'an 93:9; bikur cholim; unhu/ubuntu)
Challenging harmful beliefs, such as that prayer replaces ART, by saying that prayer and medicine belong together

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Religious organisations teach prevention. They teach abstinence before marriage and faithfulness within marriage, and encourage voluntary testing. Religions differ on condoms: the Catholic Church teaches abstinence and fidelity, while many other churches and Muslim and Jewish teachers accept condoms for protection.

Church and mission clinics offer testing and antiretroviral treatment, and congregations announce clinic days. Volunteers carry out home-based care, visiting the sick, helping with food and washing and supporting families. Congregations support orphans and vulnerable children with school fees, food and counselling, and support groups for people living with HIV often meet in church or mosque halls.

Religious leaders speak against stigma and teach compassion, drawing on Matthew 25:35-40, James 1:27, Qur'an 93:9, bikur cholim and unhu. Many leaders also challenge the harmful belief that prayer can replace ART, saying that prayer and medicine belong together.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed response, one for support groups. Credit any accurate description and mark up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far have religious teachings and organisations helped to reduce stigma against people living with HIV?

points.description: Religions teach compassion and care for the sick and orphans (Matthew 25:35-40; bikur cholim; Qur'an 93:9; unhu)
Support groups and home-based care bring people into the community and show acceptance
Leaders who speak openly against stigma and encourage testing set an example
Limits: some leaders have blamed HIV on sin or witchcraft, or told members to stop ART, which increased stigma and fear
A supported conclusion

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.
Nothing creditworthy.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Religious teachings and organisations have helped to a large extent. The four religions teach compassion and care for the sick and orphans, as in Matthew 25:35-40, bikur cholim, Qur'an 93:9 and unhu. Support groups and home-based care bring people living with HIV into the life of the community and show acceptance, and leaders who speak openly against stigma and encourage testing set an example.

However, there are limits. Some leaders have blamed HIV on sin or witchcraft, or told members to stop treatment, which increased stigma and fear and delayed testing.

I conclude that religious bodies have done more to reduce stigma than to increase it, because most teach compassion and their practical care reaches many people, but where some leaders blame the sick they undo this work. Continued teaching of compassion and accurate health information is needed.

parts.explanation: Level marking: help and limits both developed, with examples, and a supported conclusion.

explanation: A Paper 2 style question: (a) describe religious responses, (b) assess the effect on stigma.
hints: In (a) give at least five responses with a teaching behind some of them. In (b) weigh help against harm.

stem: This question is about religion and drug and substance abuse.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain the causes and effects of drug and substance abuse among young people in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Causes: peer pressure from friends who use substances
Causes: stress, unemployment and poverty, and the false belief that substances solve problems
Causes: problems at home, curiosity, loneliness and easy availability of substances such as alcohol, cough syrups (bronclee) and crystal meth (mutoriro)
Effects on the individual: damage to the brain, liver or lungs, addiction and mental health problems
Effects on the individual: poor school results, accidents and risky behaviour
Effects on the family: quarrels, violence, loss of money and trust, and neglect of children
Effects on society: crime, road accidents, unemployment and strain on health services
Developed link between cause and effect, for example that unemployed youth with no activity turn to substances and may become addicted

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Several causes lead young people to use harmful substances. Peer pressure is a major one, as friends who use drugs may pressure others to join. Stress, unemployment and poverty are others, together with the false belief that substances solve problems. Some young people use them because of problems at home, curiosity or loneliness, and substances such as alcohol, cough syrups like bronclee and crystal meth (mutoriro) are easily available.

The effects are felt at several levels. For the individual, substances damage the brain, liver and lungs, cause addiction and mental health problems, lead to poor school results, and cause accidents and risky behaviour. For the family, they cause quarrels and violence, loss of money and trust, and neglect of children. For society, they lead to crime, road accidents, unemployment and strain on health services.

The causes and effects are linked: for example, an unemployed young person with nothing to do may turn to substances, become addicted, and then lose the chance to find work.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed cause or effect, one for the effects on the individual (second point). Credit any accurate explanation up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assess the view that religious teaching is the most effective way of dealing with drug and substance abuse.

points.description: Religion gives clear teaching (Qur'an 5:90; Ephesians 5:18; moderation in Judaism and Indigenous Religion) and values that discourage substance use
Religious communities offer youth activities, counselling and support that keep young people occupied and connected
Limits: not all young people belong to a religious group, and teaching alone does not treat addiction
Other approaches are needed: health services, rehabilitation, family support, schools and law enforcement; religious bodies often work with them
A supported conclusion

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.
Nothing creditworthy.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Religious teaching is very useful but is probably not the most effective way by itself. Religions give clear teaching and values that discourage substance use, such as Qur'an 5:90, Ephesians 5:18 and the emphasis on moderation in Judaism and Indigenous Religion. Religious communities also offer youth activities, counselling and support that keep young people occupied and connected.

However, not all young people belong to a religious group, and teaching alone does not treat addiction. Health services, rehabilitation, family support, schools and law enforcement are also needed, and religious bodies often work with them.

I conclude that religion is an important part of the response, because it gives values and community, but it is most effective when it works together with health services and other agencies.

parts.explanation: Level marking: developed strengths and limits, other approaches, and a supported judgement.

explanation: A Paper 2 style question: (a) explain causes and effects, (b) assess the role of religious teaching.
hints: In (a) give causes and effects at three levels. In (b) weigh religion against other approaches.

stem: This question is about religion and life issues.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the views of two religions on abortion.

points.description: Zimbabwean law (Termination of Pregnancy Act) allows abortion only in limited circumstances, such as danger to the woman's life or health, rape or incest, or serious abnormality in the unborn child
Christianity: the Catholic Church opposes abortion from conception, citing the sanctity of life and passages such as Psalm 139:13-16 and Jeremiah 1:5
Christianity: many Protestant and other churches also oppose abortion, some allowing exceptions such as danger to the mother, and a few support wider choice
Islam: life is a gift of God, and killing is forbidden (Qur'an 17:33)
Islam: most scholars permit abortion only for serious reasons such as saving the mother's life, and mainly in early pregnancy
Islam: views differ on when the unborn child is considered alive in the full sense
Judaism (if used): the unborn child is protected but not treated as a full person until birth; abortion is permitted when the mother's life is in danger
Indigenous Religion (if used): children are a blessing from Mwari and the ancestors, and abortion is generally disapproved of

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In Zimbabwe the Termination of Pregnancy Act allows abortion only in limited circumstances, such as danger to the woman's life or health, rape or incest, or serious abnormality in the unborn child.

In Christianity the Catholic Church opposes abortion from conception, because it teaches the sanctity of life, citing passages such as Psalm 139:13-16 and Jeremiah 1:5. Many Protestant and other churches also oppose abortion, some allowing exceptions such as danger to the mother, and a few support wider choice.

In Islam life is a gift of God and killing is forbidden (Qur'an 17:33). Most scholars permit abortion only for serious reasons such as saving the mother's life, and mainly in early pregnancy, and views differ on when the unborn child is considered alive in the full sense.

Thus both religions value life, but they differ in the exceptions they allow.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed view; any two religions may be chosen. Mark the best points up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss how far the religions of Zimbabwe agree on the value of life.

points.description: They agree that life is a gift and sacred (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139; Qur'an 5:32; Mwari and the ancestors)
They generally oppose active euthanasia and support palliative care
They differ in applying the value to abortion, contraception, IVF, organ donation and blood transfusion
Views also differ within religions, for example between Catholic and other Christians, or Orthodox and Reform Jews
A supported conclusion, for example that they agree on principle but differ in application

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.
Nothing creditworthy.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The religions agree to a large extent on the principle that life is a gift and sacred. Judaism teaches that people are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), Christians cite Psalm 139, Muslims cite Qur'an 5:32, and in Indigenous Religion life comes from Mwari and the ancestors. They also generally oppose active euthanasia and support palliative care.

However, they differ in applying this value to abortion, contraception, IVF, organ donation and blood transfusion. Views differ within religions too, for example between Catholic and other Christians, and between Orthodox and Reform Jews.

I conclude that the religions agree on the principle of the value of life but differ in how to apply it to hard cases, so their agreement is real but partial.

parts.explanation: Level marking: agreement and disagreement developed with examples, and a supported conclusion.

explanation: A Paper 2 style question: (a) describe views on abortion, (b) discuss agreement on the value of life.
hints: In (a) choose two religions and give position, reason and exception. In (b) separate agreement from disagreement.

stem: This question is about religious teachings on work, wealth and poverty.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe what Indigenous Religion, Christianity and Islam teach about work and wealth.

points.description: Indigenous Religion: work is part of community life, shown in the nhimbe/ilima, and laziness is condemned
Indigenous Religion: wealth is shared, as in the chief's communal field (zunde ramambo), and greed and selfishness break unhu
Christianity: work is part of God's plan (Genesis 2:15), and 2 Thessalonians 3:10 teaches that those who refuse to work should not eat
Christianity: wealth is not wrong, but the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10), and believers are taught to give tithes and offerings and care for the poor
Islam: honest, lawful work is a form of worship (Qur'an 62:10), and Muslims are encouraged to earn by halal means
Islam: wealth is a trust from God, and Muslims must pay zakat (usually 2.5% of qualifying savings) and give sadaqah
Poverty has many causes and the poor must be helped (Deuteronomy 15:11; Proverbs 14:31), not blamed
Wastefulness and greed are warned against (Qur'an 17:26-27; Luke 12:15-21)

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In Indigenous Religion work is part of community life, as shown in the nhimbe or ilima, in which neighbours help one another, and laziness is condemned. Wealth is shared, as in the chief's communal field, the zunde ramambo, and greed and selfishness break unhu.

In Christianity work is part of God's plan, since Genesis 2:15 shows people put in the garden to work it, and 2 Thessalonians 3:10 teaches that those who refuse to work should not eat. Wealth is not wrong, but the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10). Christians give tithes and offerings and care for the poor, and in Luke 12:15-21 Jesus warns against greed.

In Islam honest, lawful work is a form of worship (Qur'an 62:10), and Muslims are encouraged to earn by halal means. Wealth is a trust from God, so Muslims pay zakat, usually 2.5% of qualifying savings, and give sadaqah. The Qur'an warns against wastefulness (Qur'an 17:26-27).

The religions also teach that poverty has many causes and that the poor must be helped, not blamed (Deuteronomy 15:11; Proverbs 14:31).

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed teaching and one for the warning about waste. Mark the best points up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: To what extent is the prosperity gospel consistent with Christian teaching?

points.description: Supporters: scripture such as Malachi 3:10 and 3 John 2 shows that God blesses; the teaching encourages hope, hard work and enterprise
Critics: it misreads the Bible, which also warns against the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10) and says the rich find it hard to enter the kingdom (Matthew 19:21-24)
Critics: it may blame the poor or sick for lacking faith and gives false hope
Critics: leaders may become rich while members give beyond their means; many Christians take a middle position that God blesses but giving does not guarantee wealth
A supported conclusion

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The prosperity gospel is consistent with some Christian teaching but not with all of it. Supporters point to scripture such as Malachi 3:10 and 3 John 2, which they say show that God blesses believers, and say the teaching encourages hope, hard work and enterprise.

Critics say it misreads the Bible, which also warns against the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10) and says that the rich find it hard to enter the kingdom (Matthew 19:21-24). They argue that it may blame the poor or sick for lacking faith, gives false hope, and may enrich leaders while members give beyond their means. Many Christians take a middle position: God blesses, but giving does not guarantee wealth.

I conclude that it is consistent with the Christian teaching that God blesses and with the encouragement of work, but not with the warnings about the love of money or with the idea that wealth proves faith.

parts.explanation: Level marking: supporters' and critics' arguments developed with texts, and a supported conclusion.

explanation: A Paper 2 style question: (a) describe teachings on work and wealth, (b) assess the prosperity gospel.
hints: In (a) cover each religion with a text or practice. In (b) give both supporters and critics with Bible references.

stem: This question is about enterprise projects run by religious organisations.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the enterprise projects run by religious organisations in Zimbabwe and explain how they serve their communities.

points.description: Farming and gardens: church or mission farms and poultry projects supply food, give work, and the surplus is sold to earn income
Education: mission schools and colleges give access to education, especially in rural areas
Health: mission hospitals and clinics serve patients of all faiths
Publishing, media and transport serve members and the public and earn fees
Skills and training centres teach sewing, carpentry, agriculture or computing to young people and women, helping them earn a living
Savings clubs (mukando), burial societies and welfare funds help members meet emergencies such as funerals without falling into debt
Other religions: Islamic waqf endowments and zakat committees, Jewish community loan funds, and Indigenous Religion's zunde ramambo and nhimbe
Income from projects pays for the work of the organisation, for example school fees for orphans

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Religious organisations in Zimbabwe run many kinds of enterprise. Church and mission farms, gardens and poultry projects supply food and give work, and the surplus is sold to earn income. Mission schools and colleges give access to education, especially in rural areas, and mission hospitals and clinics serve patients of all faiths. Some organisations run publishing, media and transport.

Skills and training centres teach sewing, carpentry, agriculture or computing to young people and women, helping them to earn a living. Savings clubs (mukando), burial societies and welfare funds help members to meet emergencies such as funerals without falling into debt.

Other religions have similar projects: Muslims use waqf endowments and zakat committees, Jewish communities keep funds for interest-free loans, and in Indigenous Religion the zunde ramambo and the nhimbe serve the community. Income from projects pays for the work of the organisation, for example school fees for orphans.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed project, one for publishing, media and transport. Mark the best points up to 15.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assess the view that religious organisations should concentrate on worship and leave enterprise to others.

points.description: For the view: business can distract from worship and the spiritual purpose of the organisation
For the view: problems such as mismanagement, lack of accountability, exploitation of followers and commercialisation of religion can harm trust
Against the view: projects meet real needs that others may not, such as rural schools, clinics and training, and put teachings on service and care into practice
Against the view: income supports the work of the organisation and creates jobs; honest records and openness reduce the risks
A supported conclusion

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is some truth in this view, but I do not think it is the best conclusion. Business can distract from worship and the spiritual purpose of an organisation, and problems such as mismanagement, lack of accountability, exploitation of followers and commercialisation of religion can harm trust.

On the other hand, projects meet real needs that others may not meet, such as rural schools, clinics and training, and they put into practice the teachings on service and care. Income supports the work of the organisation and creates jobs, and honest records and openness reduce the risks.

I conclude that religious organisations should continue with enterprise, provided that it is honest, open and accountable and remains secondary to their spiritual purpose.
